chapters.title: Accounting Standards, Framework and Applicability
chapters.summary: How Accounting Standards are made in India, what the Framework says about financial statements, and which entities must follow which standards.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 and ICAI Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements, as in force in 2026

lesson.heading: Accounting Standards and how they are made
lesson.body:
Accounting Standards (AS) are written policy documents that set out how transactions are recognised, measured, presented and disclosed. In India the **Accounting Standards Board (ASB)** of ICAI drafts them.

The usual process:

- ASB identifies the area and forms a study group.
- A preliminary draft is discussed with specified bodies (regulators, industry associations) and an **Exposure Draft** is issued for public comment.
- Comments are considered and the final draft goes to the **ICAI Council** for approval.
- For companies, the **Central Government notifies** standards under **section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013** after consulting the **National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA)**. The standards that apply to non-Ind AS companies are now in the **Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021**.

India has two sets: **Ind AS** (converged with IFRS, with a few **carve-outs**, i.e. departures from IFRS for Indian conditions) and **AS** (the older standards). This paper (Inter P1) tests AS; Ind AS is a Final subject.

| Point | Convergence | Adoption |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Meaning | Standards brought close to IFRS, with local changes | IFRS taken as issued |
| India | Ind AS (converged, with carve-outs) | Not followed |

lesson.heading: The Framework in brief
lesson.body:
The **Framework for the Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements** is not an AS. It guides standard setters and preparers where no AS applies. If the Framework and an AS conflict, the AS prevails.

- **Users**: investors, employees, lenders, suppliers, customers, government, public.
- **Underlying assumptions**: going concern, accrual, consistency.
- **Qualitative characteristics**: understandability, relevance, reliability, comparability (materiality is a threshold for relevance).
- **Elements**: asset, liability, equity, income, expenses.
- **Recognition**: an item is recognised when it is probable that future economic benefit will flow and it has a cost or value that can be measured reliably.
- **Measurement bases**: historical cost, current cost, realisable (settlement) value, present value.

**Capital maintenance** decides what profit is. Profit is the excess of closing capital over opening capital (after owner transactions):

| Concept | Capital to be maintained |
| --- | --- |
| Financial capital (money) | Opening equity in nominal rupees |
| Financial capital (constant purchasing power) | Opening equity x general price index change |
| Physical capital | Operating capacity, measured at current replacement cost |

lesson.heading: Who applies which standards
Worked example: capital maintenance
lesson.body:
A trader starts with ₹10,00,000 cash, buys 1,000 units at ₹1,000 and sells all of them for ₹13,00,000. The general price index rises from 100 to 110 during the year. Replacement cost at year end is ₹1,200 per unit.

| Concept | Closing capital | Capital to maintain | Profit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Financial (nominal) | 13,00,000 | 10,00,000 | 3,00,000 |
| Financial (constant purchasing power) | 13,00,000 | 11,00,000 | 2,00,000 |
| Physical | 13,00,000 | 12,00,000 | 1,00,000 |

The ₹1,00,000 under CPP and ₹2,00,000 under physical capital are capital maintenance adjustments, credited to equity, not profit.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Treating the Framework as an Accounting Standard. It is guidance and gives way to an AS.
- Saying ICAI notifies AS for companies. ICAI formulates; the Central Government notifies under section 133.
- Testing SMC status on current-year figures. The turnover and borrowing tests use the **immediately preceding** accounting year, and borrowings are tested **at any time** during that year, not only at year end.
- Forgetting that a subsidiary of a non-SMC is never an SMC, however small.
- Calling prudence a licence for secret reserves. The Framework rejects deliberate understatement.

keyPoints: ASB of ICAI formulates AS; Central Government notifies them for companies under section 133 after consulting NFRA.
Framework: assumptions going concern, accrual, consistency; QCs understandability, relevance, reliability, comparability.
Five elements: asset, liability, equity, income, expenses.
Measurement bases: historical cost, current cost, realisable value, present value.
Profit depends on capital maintenance: financial (nominal or CPP) or physical (current cost).
SMC: unlisted, not bank/FI/insurer, preceding-year turnover up to ₹250 crore, borrowings up to ₹50 crore at any time, not holding/subsidiary of a non-SMC.

cases.body:
Vardhan Traders started business on 1 April 2026 with equity capital of ₹20,00,000, all in cash. On the same day it bought 4,000 units of a product at ₹500 each. By 31 March 2027 it had sold all 4,000 units for ₹26,00,000 in cash. There were no other transactions.

| Data | Value |
| --- | --- |
| General price index on 1 April 2026 | 120 |
| General price index on 31 March 2027 | 132 |
| Replacement cost per unit on 31 March 2027 | ₹560 |

questions.prompt: Under the Companies Act, 2013, who prescribes the Accounting Standards that companies must follow?
options: The Central Government, in consultation with NFRA
The ICAI Council, without government involvement
The Registrar of Companies of each state
questions.explanation: Section 133 empowers the Central Government to prescribe standards as recommended by ICAI, in consultation with NFRA. ICAI formulates them; notification is by the government.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a principal qualitative characteristic of financial statements under the Framework?
questions.explanation: The four principal qualitative characteristics are understandability, relevance, reliability and comparability. Profitability is a result, not a quality of information.

questions.prompt: Assets carried at the amount of cash that could currently be obtained by selling them in an orderly disposal are measured at:
questions.explanation: Realisable value is the cash obtainable by an orderly sale; for liabilities the equivalent is settlement value. Current cost is the cost to acquire the same asset now.

questions.prompt: Which set lists the fundamental accounting assumptions under AS 1 and the Framework?
questions.explanation: Going concern, consistency and accrual are the fundamental assumptions. If one is not followed, the fact must be disclosed. Prudence, substance over form and materiality are considerations in selecting policies.

questions.prompt: The prudence concept in the Framework permits an enterprise to create secret reserves by deliberately understating income.
questions.explanation: Prudence means caution in judgements under uncertainty. It does not allow deliberate understatement of assets or income or overstatement of liabilities, because that makes statements unreliable.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are elements of financial statements as defined in the Framework? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The Framework defines five elements: asset, liability and equity (financial position) and income and expenses (performance). Cash flow is reported but is not a defined element.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the assumption that an enterprise will continue in operation for the foreseeable future is the ___ assumption.
questions.explanation: Going concern means there is neither the intention nor the need to liquidate or curtail operations materially, so assets are not carried at break-up values.

questions.prompt: Compute the profit for 2026-27 under the financial capital maintenance concept in nominal monetary units. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Closing capital (cash) | 26,00,000 |
| Less: Opening capital in nominal terms | (20,00,000) |
| **Profit** | **6,00,000** |

questions.prompt: Compute the profit under the financial capital maintenance concept in units of constant purchasing power. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
Capital to maintain = 20,00,000 x 132/120 = ₹22,00,000.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Closing capital | 26,00,000 |
| Less: Opening capital restated | (22,00,000) |
| **Profit** | **4,00,000** |

The ₹2,00,000 restatement is a capital maintenance adjustment in equity.

questions.prompt: Compute the profit under the physical capital maintenance concept. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
To maintain operating capacity the business must be able to buy back 4,000 units at ₹560 = ₹22,40,000.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Closing capital | 26,00,000 |
| Less: Capital to maintain physical capacity | (22,40,000) |
| **Profit** | **3,60,000** |

questions.prompt: Which capital maintenance concept requires Vardhan Traders to measure its capital using the current cost basis?
options: Financial capital maintenance in nominal units
Financial capital maintenance in constant purchasing power
None; the Framework allows only historical cost
questions.explanation: Physical capital is productive capacity, which is measured by what it costs today to replace the inputs. Financial capital can be measured in nominal or constant purchasing power units without current cost.

questions.prompt: Which of these companies qualifies as a Small and Medium-sized Company (SMC) for 2026-27? All figures relate to 2025-26 and none is a bank, FI or insurer.
options: Unlisted private company: turnover ₹240 crore, maximum borrowings during the year ₹45 crore, not a holding or subsidiary of a non-SMC
Unlisted public company: turnover ₹120 crore, borrowings ₹62 crore on one day in October, ₹30 crore at year end
Private company: turnover ₹40 crore, no borrowings, wholly owned subsidiary of a listed company
Company with turnover ₹20 crore whose equity shares are in the process of listing on a stock exchange
questions.explanation: Only the first meets every test. The second crossed ₹50 crore borrowings at some time during the year. The third is a subsidiary of a non-SMC (a listed company). The fourth is in the process of listing.

questions.prompt: Explain the process followed in India for formulating Accounting Standards.
questions.answer:
- The Accounting Standards Board (ASB) of ICAI identifies areas needing a standard and sets up study groups.
- The study group prepares a preliminary draft, considering IFRS/Ind AS, Indian laws and practice.
- ASB discusses the draft with representatives of specified bodies such as regulators, industry chambers and government departments.
- An Exposure Draft is issued for public comment; ASB considers the comments and finalises the draft.
- The final draft is submitted to the ICAI Council, which may modify and approves the standard.
- For companies, the standard is recommended to the Central Government, which notifies it under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013 after consulting NFRA (now part of the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021). For non-company entities, ICAI announces applicability.

chapters.title: AS on Assets and Inventories (AS 2, 10, 13, 16, 26, 28)
chapters.summary: Value inventories, property, plant and equipment, borrowing costs, investments, intangibles and impairment as the asset-based Accounting Standards require.
chapters.lawAsOf: AS 2, AS 10, AS 13, AS 16, AS 26 and AS 28 as notified in the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021

lesson.heading: AS 2: Valuation of inventories
lesson.body:
Inventories are valued at the **lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV)**, item by item or by groups of similar items.

- **Cost** = cost of purchase (price, duties not recoverable, freight, less trade discounts) + cost of conversion (direct labour, variable and fixed production overheads) + other costs to bring inventory to its present location and condition.
- **Fixed production overheads** are absorbed on **normal capacity**. Unabsorbed overhead from low production is an expense of the period. If actual production is higher than normal, the actual production is used so inventory is not above cost.
- **Excluded from cost**: abnormal wastage, storage costs (unless needed in the production process before a further stage), administrative overheads not contributing to present location and condition, selling and distribution costs.
- **NRV** = estimated selling price less estimated costs of completion and costs to sell.
- **Raw materials** are not written down below cost if the finished goods in which they will be used are expected to sell at or above cost. If they are written down, replacement cost may be the best measure of NRV.
- Cost formulas: FIFO or weighted average cost. Specific identification for items not ordinarily interchangeable.

AS 2 does not apply to WIP under construction contracts (AS 7), shares and other financial instruments held as stock-in-trade, and producers' livestock, agricultural and forest products and mineral ores measured at NRV under trade practice.

lesson.heading: AS 10 (PPE) and AS 16 (Borrowing costs)
lesson.body:
**AS 10**: an item of PPE is recognised when future economic benefits are probable and cost can be measured reliably. Cost includes purchase price (with non-refundable duties, less discounts), directly attributable costs (site preparation, delivery, installation, testing, professional fees) and the initial estimate of **dismantling and site restoration** cost. Opening ceremonies, advertising, administration and initial operating losses are excluded.

- After recognition: **cost model** or **revaluation model** for an entire class.
- Revaluation increase goes to **revaluation surplus** in owners' equity, except to the extent it reverses a decrease earlier charged to profit or loss. A decrease goes to profit or loss, except to the extent of an existing surplus for the same asset.
- Each significant component is depreciated separately.

**AS 16**: borrowing costs directly attributable to a **qualifying asset** (one that takes a substantial period, ordinarily 12 months or more, to get ready for use or sale) are capitalised.

- **Specific borrowings**: actual cost less income on temporary investment of those funds.
- **General borrowings**: weighted average rate of general borrowings (capitalisation rate) x weighted expenditure on the asset; capped at actual general borrowing cost.
- Capitalisation starts when expenditure, borrowing costs and activities to prepare the asset are all in progress; is suspended during extended periods of interruption; ceases when substantially all activities are complete.

lesson.heading: AS 13, AS 26 and AS 28
lesson.body:
**AS 13 Investments**: current investments at the **lower of cost and fair value** (category-wise or individually, not on overall portfolio). Long-term investments at **cost**, less provision for a **decline other than temporary**. On reclassification from long-term to current, transfer at lower of cost and carrying amount; from current to long-term, at lower of cost and fair value.

**AS 26 Intangible assets**: research expenditure is expensed. Development expenditure is capitalised only when the enterprise can show technical feasibility, intention to complete, ability to use or sell, how the asset will generate benefits, adequate resources, and reliable measurement. Internally generated goodwill, brands and mastheads are not recognised. There is a rebuttable presumption that useful life does not exceed **10 years** from the date the asset is available for use.

**AS 28 Impairment**: an asset is impaired when its carrying amount exceeds its **recoverable amount** = higher of **net selling price** and **value in use** (present value of future cash flows). The loss goes to profit or loss, or against revaluation surplus for a revalued asset.

lesson.heading: Worked example: general borrowings under AS 16
lesson.body:
General borrowings outstanding all year: 12% loan ₹10,00,000 and 10% loan ₹15,00,000. A factory (qualifying asset) is financed from these. Spending: ₹6,00,000 on 1 April and ₹4,00,000 on 1 October. Year ends 31 March.

Capitalisation rate = (1,20,000 + 1,50,000) / 25,00,000 = **10.8%**

| Date | Spent (₹) | Months | Weighted (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 April | 6,00,000 | 12/12 | 6,00,000 |
| 1 October | 4,00,000 | 6/12 | 2,00,000 |
| **Total** | | | **8,00,000** |

Borrowing cost capitalised = 8,00,000 x 10.8% = **₹86,400**. The rest of the ₹2,70,000 interest is expensed.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Absorbing fixed overheads on actual production when it is below normal capacity. Use normal capacity and expense the unabsorbed part.
- Writing down raw materials when finished goods still sell above cost.
- Capitalising interest on the full borrowing for the full year when spending happened during the year.
- Forgetting to deduct income on temporary investment of specific borrowings.
- Comparing carrying amount with net selling price only. Recoverable amount is the **higher** of NSP and value in use.
- Carrying current investments at fair value when it is above cost.

keyPoints: AS 2: lower of cost and NRV; fixed overheads on normal capacity; selling, admin and abnormal waste excluded.
Raw materials are not written down if the finished product sells at or above cost.
AS 10: cost includes initial estimate of dismantling; revaluation surplus goes to equity.
AS 16: specific borrowing cost less temporary investment income; general borrowing = capitalisation rate x weighted expenditure.
AS 13: current investments at lower of cost and fair value; long-term at cost less permanent decline.
AS 26: research expensed; development capitalised on six criteria; 10-year presumption.
AS 28: recoverable amount = higher of net selling price and value in use.

cases.title: Case: Kaveri Polymers Ltd
cases.body:
Kaveri Polymers Ltd makes one product. Data for the year ended 31 March 2027:

| Item | Data |
| --- | --- |
| Raw material in stock | 5,000 kg at cost ₹200 per kg; replacement cost ₹180 per kg |
| Finished goods in stock | 2,000 units |
| Material cost per unit | ₹300 |
| Direct labour per unit | ₹100 |
| Variable production overhead per unit | ₹50 |
| Fixed production overheads for the year | ₹24,00,000 |
| Normal capacity | 40,000 units |
| Actual production | 30,000 units |
| Expected selling price per unit | ₹560 |
| Selling costs per unit | ₹30 |

A moulding machine has a carrying amount of ₹40,00,000. Its net selling price is ₹32,00,000 and its value in use is ₹35,00,000.

questions.prompt: Under AS 2, which of the following is included in the cost of inventories?
options: Storage costs necessary in the production process before a further production stage
Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing inventory to its present location
questions.explanation: Storage is normally excluded, but storage that is a necessary part of production (for example, maturing before the next stage) is included. The other three are always excluded.

questions.prompt: A qualifying asset under AS 16 is one that:
options: Necessarily takes a substantial period of time (ordinarily 12 months or more) to get ready for its intended use or sale
Is financed wholly by specific borrowings
Is inventory manufactured in large quantities on a repetitive basis
questions.explanation: AS 16 defines a qualifying asset by the time needed to get it ready, ordinarily 12 months or more. Inventories routinely produced in large quantities over short periods are not qualifying assets.

questions.prompt: Under AS 26, expenditure on research (the research phase of an internal project) is:
options: Recognised as an expense when incurred
Capitalised once technical feasibility is shown
Deferred until the project is abandoned or completed
questions.explanation: No intangible asset arises from research because the enterprise cannot show that future benefits are probable. Only development expenditure meeting all the criteria can be capitalised.

questions.prompt: Under AS 13, current investments are carried in the financial statements at:
options: Lower of cost and fair value
Cost less provision for permanent decline
Fair value, with gains taken to profit
questions.explanation: Current investments are at the lower of cost and fair value, computed individually or by category. Cost less provision for a decline other than temporary applies to long-term investments.

questions.prompt: Under AS 10, an increase in carrying amount on first revaluation of land is credited to the Statement of Profit and Loss.
questions.explanation: A revaluation increase is credited directly to owners' interests under the heading revaluation surplus. It goes to profit or loss only to the extent it reverses a revaluation decrease of the same asset previously recognised in profit or loss.

questions.prompt: Which of the following form part of the cost of an item of PPE under AS 10? Select all that apply.
options: Initial estimate of dismantling and site restoration costs
Cost of the opening ceremony of the new plant
Initial operating losses while demand builds up
questions.explanation: Purchase price with non-refundable duties, directly attributable costs such as site preparation and installation, and the initial estimate of dismantling are included. Opening ceremonies and initial operating losses are not necessary to bring the asset to working condition.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under AS 28, recoverable amount is the higher of an asset's net selling price and its ___.
questions.explanation: Value in use is the present value of estimated future cash flows from continuing use and disposal at the end of useful life.

questions.prompt: At what amount should the finished goods stock be valued at 31 March 2027? Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
Fixed overhead per unit on normal capacity = 24,00,000 / 40,000 = ₹60.

| Cost per unit | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Material | 300 |
| Labour | 100 |
| Variable overhead | 50 |
| Fixed overhead | 60 |
| **Cost** | **510** |

NRV = 560 - 30 = ₹530. Lower of cost and NRV = ₹510. Value = 2,000 x 510 = **₹10,20,000**.

questions.prompt: What amount of fixed production overhead must be recognised as an expense of the year (unabsorbed overhead)? Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: Absorbed = 30,000 units x ₹60 = ₹18,00,000. Unabsorbed = 24,00,000 - 18,00,000 = **₹6,00,000**, charged to profit or loss because production was below normal capacity.

questions.prompt: At what amount should the raw material stock be valued?
options: ₹10,00,000, because the finished goods are expected to sell above cost
₹9,50,000, the average of cost and replacement cost
₹9,00,000, because replacement cost is always NRV for raw materials
questions.explanation: Raw materials are not written down below cost when the finished product will sell at or above cost. Finished goods cost ₹510 and NRV is ₹530, so raw material stays at 5,000 x ₹200 = ₹10,00,000.

questions.prompt: Compute the impairment loss on the moulding machine under AS 28. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: Recoverable amount = higher of NSP ₹32,00,000 and value in use ₹35,00,000 = ₹35,00,000. Impairment loss = 40,00,000 - 35,00,000 = **₹5,00,000**.

questions.prompt: On 1 April 2026 a company borrowed ₹50,00,000 at 12% p.a. specifically to build a warehouse (a qualifying asset), completed on 31 March 2027. Funds not yet needed were temporarily invested and earned ₹40,000. How much borrowing cost is capitalised for 2026-27? Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Interest 50,00,000 x 12% | 6,00,000 |
| Less: Income on temporary investment | (40,000) |
| **Capitalised** | **5,60,000** |

questions.prompt: Compute the borrowing cost to be capitalised for 2026-27 under AS 16 and the amount charged to profit or loss.
questions.data: General borrowings outstanding throughout 2026-27: 11% term loan ₹20,00,000 and 9% debentures ₹30,00,000. A building (qualifying asset) is financed from general funds. Spending on the building: ₹10,00,000 on 1 April 2026, ₹8,00,000 on 1 July 2026 and ₹6,00,000 on 1 January 2027. Construction continues beyond 31 March 2027.

chapters.title: AS on Revenue, Liabilities and Provisions (AS 4, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 22, 29)
chapters.summary: Recognise revenue and contract profits, government grants, provisions, post-balance-sheet events, employee benefits and deferred tax under the Accounting Standards.
chapters.lawAsOf: AS 4, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 22 and 29 as notified in the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021

lesson.heading: AS 9 and AS 7: revenue and construction contracts
lesson.body:
**AS 9**: revenue from sale of goods is recognised when the seller has transferred the significant risks and rewards of ownership, has no effective control over the goods, and there is no significant uncertainty about the consideration. Services: proportionate completion or completed service contract method. Interest on time proportion basis, royalties on accrual, dividends when the right to receive is established.

**AS 7**: when the outcome of a construction contract can be estimated reliably, revenue and costs are recognised by **stage of completion** (percentage of completion method), commonly measured as cost incurred to date / total estimated cost.

- When it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total revenue, the **expected loss is recognised as an expense immediately**, whatever the stage of completion.
- When the outcome cannot be estimated reliably, revenue is recognised only to the extent of recoverable costs incurred.

| Step | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Stage of completion | Cost to date / (Cost to date + Estimated cost to complete) |
| Revenue recognised | Contract price x Stage |
| Profit (if profitable) | Revenue - Cost of work done |
| Loss (if loss-making) | Full expected loss now |

lesson.heading: AS 12, AS 29 and AS 4
lesson.body:
**AS 12 Government grants** are recognised when there is reasonable assurance that the conditions will be met and the grant will be received.

- Grant in the nature of **promoters' contribution**: credited to **capital reserve** (capital approach).
- Grant for a specific depreciable asset: either **deducted from the gross value** of the asset, or treated as **deferred income** taken to profit and loss over the useful life in proportion to depreciation.
- Grant for a non-depreciable asset with no obligation: capital reserve.
- Revenue grants: income over the periods of related costs.

**AS 29**: a **provision** is recognised when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow is probable, and a reliable estimate can be made. A **contingent liability** is disclosed (unless remote). A **contingent asset** is not recognised; it is usually disclosed in the report of the approving authority. No provision for future operating losses.

**AS 4**: events after the balance sheet date that give evidence of conditions **existing at** the balance sheet date are **adjusting** (for example insolvency of a debtor who was already in difficulty). Events about conditions arising **after** that date are **non-adjusting** and disclosed if material. Dividends proposed or declared after the balance sheet date are **not** recognised as a liability.

lesson.heading: AS 5, AS 15 and AS 22
lesson.body:
**AS 5**: prior period items are income or expenses arising in the current period from **errors or omissions** in earlier periods; shown separately. A **change in accounting estimate** (for example useful life) is not a prior period item; its effect goes to current and future periods. A **change in accounting policy** is made only if required by statute or an AS, or for a more appropriate presentation.

**AS 15 Employee benefits**: short-term benefits are expensed as the service is rendered. Post-employment plans:

- **Defined contribution** (for example provident fund to a government scheme): expense = contribution payable.
- **Defined benefit** (for example gratuity): liability = present value of defined benefit obligation **less** fair value of plan assets, using the **projected unit credit method**. Under AS 15, actuarial gains and losses are recognised **immediately in profit or loss**.

**AS 22 Taxes on income**: tax expense = current tax + deferred tax. Deferred tax arises only on **timing differences** (originate in one period, reverse later), not on permanent differences. Deferred tax assets need **reasonable certainty** of future taxable income; where there are unabsorbed depreciation or carried forward losses, **virtual certainty supported by convincing evidence**. Use rates enacted or substantively enacted at the balance sheet date.

lesson.heading: Worked example: AS 7
lesson.body:
Fixed-price contract ₹1,00,00,000. Cost to date ₹42,00,000; estimated further cost ₹28,00,000.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Total estimated cost | 70,00,000 |
| Stage of completion = 42 / 70 | 60% |
| Revenue = 1,00,00,000 x 60% | 60,00,000 |
| Less: Cost of work done | (42,00,000) |
| **Profit recognised** | **18,00,000** |

If total estimated cost had been ₹1,10,00,000, the full expected loss of ₹10,00,000 would be recognised now.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Recognising only the 'stage' share of an expected loss. AS 7 needs the whole expected loss now.
- Treating a final dividend proposed after year end as a current liability.
- Creating deferred tax on permanent differences such as penalties or exempt income.
- Taking actuarial losses on gratuity to reserves. Under AS 15 they go to profit or loss.
- Recognising a contingent asset because it is probable. Only when realisation is virtually certain is the asset no longer contingent.
- Calling a revised useful life a prior period item.

keyPoints: AS 7: stage = cost to date / total estimated cost; expected loss recognised in full immediately.
AS 9: goods when significant risks and rewards pass and no significant uncertainty on consideration.
AS 12: promoters' contribution grant to capital reserve; depreciable asset grant deducted from cost or deferred income.
AS 29: provision = present obligation + probable outflow + reliable estimate; contingent assets not recognised.
AS 4: proposed dividends after the balance sheet date are not a liability.
AS 15: DB liability = PV of DBO - FV of plan assets; actuarial gains and losses in profit or loss.
AS 22: deferred tax on timing differences only; virtual certainty for DTA on unabsorbed depreciation and losses.

cases.title: Case: Neelkanth Infra Ltd
cases.body:
Neelkanth Infra Ltd signed a fixed-price contract on 1 April 2026 to build a bridge for ₹2,40,00,000. Details at 31 March 2027 (end of year 1):

| Item | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Contract costs incurred to date (all relating to work done) | 90,00,000 |
| Estimated further costs to complete | 1,60,00,000 |

The outcome of the contract can be estimated reliably. The company measures stage of completion by the cost incurred to date as a proportion of total estimated cost.

questions.prompt: Under AS 9, revenue from the sale of goods is recognised when:
options: Significant risks and rewards of ownership have passed to the buyer and there is no significant uncertainty about the consideration
The sale order is received from the customer
Cash is received from the customer
Goods are manufactured and ready for despatch
questions.explanation: AS 9 ties recognition to transfer of significant risks and rewards (and loss of effective control) with no significant uncertainty about collection. Order, production or cash receipt alone does not meet it.

questions.prompt: Which of the following events after the balance sheet date (31 March) is an adjusting event under AS 4?
options: Insolvency in May of a debtor who was already in serious financial difficulty at 31 March
Destruction of a warehouse by fire in April
A fall in the market value of investments in May caused by events in May
Declaration of a final dividend by the board in May
questions.explanation: The debtor's insolvency confirms a condition (inability to pay) that existed at the balance sheet date, so the receivable is adjusted. The fire and market fall relate to conditions arising later. Dividends after year end are not a liability.

questions.prompt: A government grant given as promoters' contribution towards the total capital outlay of a new project, with no repayment obligation, is accounted for under AS 12 by:
options: Crediting it to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the year of receipt
Deducting it from the cost of plant only
Showing it as a current liability
questions.explanation: Grants in the nature of promoters' contribution are treated as part of shareholders' funds (capital approach) and credited to capital reserve.

questions.prompt: A company has unabsorbed depreciation under tax laws. Under AS 22, a deferred tax asset on it can be recognised only when:
options: There is virtual certainty, supported by convincing evidence, of sufficient future taxable income
There is reasonable certainty of future taxable income
The tax rate is expected to rise
questions.explanation: For unabsorbed depreciation and carry forward losses, AS 22 needs virtual certainty backed by convincing evidence, a stricter test than the reasonable certainty used for other timing differences.

questions.prompt: Under AS 29, a provision should be recognised for operating losses expected in the next financial year.
questions.explanation: Future operating losses do not arise from a past event and there is no present obligation, so no provision is made. They may indicate impairment under AS 28.

questions.prompt: Under AS 29, which conditions must ALL be met before a provision is recognised? Select all that apply.
options: The enterprise has a present obligation as a result of a past event
It is probable that an outflow of resources will be required to settle it
A reliable estimate of the amount can be made
Management intends to spend the money in future
The obligation depends on future actions of the enterprise
questions.explanation: Present obligation from a past event, probable outflow and reliable estimate are the three conditions. An intention, or an obligation the enterprise can avoid by future actions, is not a present obligation.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under AS 22, differences between taxable income and accounting income that originate in one period and reverse in later periods are called ___ differences.
questions.explanation: Timing differences create deferred tax. Permanent differences originate in one period and never reverse, so they create no deferred tax.

questions.prompt: Compute the stage of completion at 31 March 2027. Answer as a percentage, rounded to the nearest whole number.
Compute the contract revenue to be recognised for the year ended 31 March 2027. Answer in rupees.
Compute the total loss to be recognised on the contract in the Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended 31 March 2027. Enter the loss as a positive figure in rupees.
questions.explanation: Expected loss = Total cost 2,50,00,000 - Contract price 2,40,00,000 = ₹10,00,000. AS 7 requires the full expected loss to be recognised immediately, so the year 1 loss is **₹10,00,000**, not 36% of it.

questions.prompt: What is the provision for foreseeable (future) loss to be created at 31 March 2027, over and above the loss on work done to date?
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue recognised | 86,40,000 |
| Less: Cost of work done | (90,00,000) |
| Loss on work done | (3,60,000) |
| Provision for future loss (balancing) | (6,40,000) |
| **Total expected loss** | **(10,00,000)** |

questions.prompt: For 2026-27 a company's depreciation is ₹8,00,000 in the books and ₹12,00,000 under tax law. A penalty of ₹2,00,000 charged in the books is not deductible for tax. Tax rate is 25%. Compute the deferred tax liability to be created for the year. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: Timing difference = 12,00,000 - 8,00,000 = ₹4,00,000 (reverses in later years). DTL = 4,00,000 x 25% = **₹1,00,000**. The penalty is a permanent difference and creates no deferred tax.

questions.prompt: From the actuarial data for a gratuity plan (defined benefit), compute the expense to be recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss under AS 15 and the net liability in the Balance Sheet at 31 March 2027.
questions.data:
| Item | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| PV of obligation, 1 April 2026 | 20,00,000 |
| Current service cost | 3,00,000 |
| Interest cost (8% on opening obligation) | 1,60,000 |
| Benefits paid | 2,00,000 |
| PV of obligation, 31 March 2027 (actuary) | 24,00,000 |
| Fair value of plan assets, 1 April 2026 | 15,00,000 |
| Expected return on plan assets (9%) | 1,35,000 |
| Contributions paid by employer | 4,00,000 |
| Fair value of plan assets, 31 March 2027 | 18,00,000 |
questions.answer:
**Obligation**

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Opening PV of obligation | 20,00,000 |
| Add: Current service cost | 3,00,000 |
| Add: Interest cost | 1,60,000 |
| Less: Benefits paid | (2,00,000) |
| Expected closing obligation | 22,60,000 |
| Actual closing obligation | 24,00,000 |
| **Actuarial loss on obligation** | **1,40,000** |

**Plan assets**

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Opening fair value | 15,00,000 |
| Add: Contributions | 4,00,000 |
| Less: Benefits paid | (2,00,000) |
| Add: Actual return (balancing) | 1,00,000 |
| Closing fair value | 18,00,000 |

Actuarial loss on assets = Expected return 1,35,000 - Actual return 1,00,000 = ₹35,000.

**Expense in Statement of Profit and Loss**

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Current service cost | 3,00,000 |
| Interest cost | 1,60,000 |
| Less: Expected return on plan assets | (1,35,000) |
| Actuarial loss (1,40,000 + 35,000) | 1,75,000 |
| **Total expense** | **5,00,000** |

**Net liability** = 24,00,000 - 18,00,000 = **₹6,00,000**.

Check: opening net liability 5,00,000 + expense 5,00,000 - contributions 4,00,000 = 6,00,000.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between prior period items and changes in accounting estimates under AS 5, with an example of each.
questions.answer:
- **Prior period items** are income or expenses that arise in the current period because of errors or omissions in preparing financial statements of one or more earlier periods. Example: depreciation omitted on a machine in the previous year, detected now.
- They are shown separately in the Statement of Profit and Loss so their effect on current profit is visible.
- **Changes in accounting estimates** arise from new information or more experience, not from errors. Example: revising the remaining useful life of a machine from 8 to 5 years, or revising a bad debt estimate.
- The effect of a change in estimate goes into profit or loss of the period of change and future periods if affected, under the same head as the original item; it is not a prior period item.
- If it is hard to tell a change in policy from a change in estimate, AS 5 treats it as a change in estimate, with disclosure.

chapters.title: AS on Presentation and Disclosure (AS 1, 3, 17, 18, 19, 20, 24, 25)
chapters.summary: Apply the presentation and disclosure standards: accounting policies, cash flow statements, EPS, segment reporting, related parties, leases, discontinuing operations and interim reporting.
chapters.lawAsOf: AS 1, 3, 17, 18, 19, 20, 24 and 25 as notified in the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021

lesson.heading: AS 1 and AS 3
lesson.body:
**AS 1 Disclosure of accounting policies**: all significant accounting policies are disclosed in one place, usually the first note. Major considerations in selecting policies are **prudence, substance over form and materiality**. If a fundamental assumption (going concern, consistency, accrual) is not followed, that fact is disclosed. A wrong treatment is not cured by disclosure.

**AS 3 Cash flow statements** classify cash flows into:

| Activity | Examples (non-financial enterprise) |
| --- | --- |
| Operating | Receipts from customers, payments to suppliers and employees, income tax paid (unless linked to investing or financing) |
| Investing | Purchase or sale of PPE and investments, interest and dividends received |
| Financing | Issue or buyback of shares, borrowings and repayments, interest paid, dividends paid |

Operating cash flow can be shown by the **direct** or **indirect** method. Indirect method: profit before tax, add back non-cash items (depreciation), remove investing and financing items (profit on sale of assets, interest expense), adjust working capital changes, then deduct tax paid.

lesson.heading: AS 20 Earnings per share
lesson.body:
**Basic EPS** = Net profit attributable to equity shareholders (after preference dividend and its tax) / Weighted average equity shares outstanding.

- **Fresh issue at full price**: weighted by time outstanding.
- **Bonus issue, share split, consolidation**: no new resources, so treated as if it happened at the start of the earliest period presented; prior EPS restated.
- **Rights issue below fair value**: has a bonus element. Adjustment factor = Fair value per share before rights (cum-rights) / Theoretical ex-rights fair value (TERP). Shares before the issue are multiplied by this factor; prior-year EPS is divided by it.

TERP = (Fair value of all shares before exercise + Rights proceeds) / Shares outstanding after exercise.

**Diluted EPS**: add back to earnings the after-tax interest on dilutive potential shares (such as convertible debentures) and add the potential shares to the denominator. A potential share is included only if it reduces EPS (is dilutive).

lesson.heading: AS 17, AS 18, AS 24, AS 25
lesson.body:
**AS 17 Segment reporting** (not for SMCs): a business or geographical segment is **reportable** if, for most of its revenue from external customers, it meets any one test:

- segment revenue (external + internal) is 10% or more of total revenue of all segments;
- segment result (profit or loss) is 10% or more of the greater of total profit of profit-making segments and total loss of loss-making segments (absolute);
- segment assets are 10% or more of total assets of all segments.

If reportable segments' external revenue is below 75% of enterprise revenue, more segments are added until 75% is reached.

**AS 18 Related party disclosures**: parties are related if one controls or significantly influences the other. Includes holding, subsidiaries, associates, JVs, key management personnel (KMP) and their relatives. Not related merely because of being a major customer, supplier or financier. Disclose relationship, nature and volume of transactions, outstanding balances.

**AS 24 Discontinuing operations**: disclosures start from the **initial disclosure event** (binding sale agreement or board approval and announcement of a plan).

**AS 25 Interim financial reporting**: each interim period is part of the annual period (integral approach for tax). Income tax expense uses the **estimated weighted average annual effective rate**.

lesson.heading: AS 19 Leases and a worked EPS example
lesson.body:
**AS 19**: a **finance lease** transfers substantially all risks and rewards incidental to ownership; otherwise it is an **operating lease**. Lessee under a finance lease records an asset and liability at the **lower of fair value and present value of minimum lease payments**; each payment is split into finance charge and principal. Operating lease payments are expensed on a straight-line basis (unless another systematic basis is more representative).

**Worked example (rights issue)**: profit 2025-26 ₹30,00,000; 2026-27 ₹44,00,000. 10,00,000 shares. Rights issue 1 for 4 at ₹40 on 1 October 2026; fair value before the rights ₹60.

| Step | Working | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TERP | (10,00,000 x 60 + 2,50,000 x 40) / 12,50,000 | ₹56 |
| Adjustment factor | 60 / 56 | 1.0714 |
| Restated EPS 2025-26 | 3.00 / 1.0714 | ₹2.80 |
| Weighted shares 2026-27 | 10,00,000 x 1.0714 x 6/12 + 12,50,000 x 6/12 | 11,60,714 |
| EPS 2026-27 | 44,00,000 / 11,60,714 | ₹3.79 |

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Weighting bonus shares from the date of issue. Bonus shares are treated as outstanding from the beginning.
- Adding back pre-tax interest for diluted EPS. Add back interest **net of tax**.
- Showing interest paid by a manufacturing company under operating activities. Under AS 3 it is financing for a non-financial enterprise.
- Applying the segment result test to total net profit. Use the greater of total profits and total losses in absolute terms.
- Treating a major customer as a related party.

keyPoints: AS 1: prudence, substance over form, materiality; disclosure does not cure wrong treatment.
AS 3 (non-financial enterprise): interest and dividends received = investing; interest and dividends paid = financing.
AS 20: bonus treated as from start of earliest period; rights factor = cum-rights fair value / TERP.
Diluted EPS: add after-tax interest and potential shares, only if dilutive.
AS 17: 10% revenue, result or assets tests; reportable segments must cover 75% of external revenue.
AS 19 finance lease: asset and liability at lower of fair value and PV of minimum lease payments.
AS 25: interim tax at estimated weighted average annual effective rate.

cases.title: Case: Suryodaya Textiles Ltd
cases.body:
Suryodaya Textiles Ltd reports net profit after tax of ₹60,00,000 for 2026-27 (no preference shares). Share data:

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| 1 April 2026 | 20,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each outstanding |
| 1 October 2026 | 4,00,000 equity shares issued for cash at full market price |
| 1 January 2027 | Bonus issue of 1 share for every 4 shares held |

10% convertible debentures of ₹1,00,00,000 (1,00,000 debentures of ₹100 each) were outstanding throughout the year. Each debenture converts into 5 equity shares (terms already adjusted for the bonus). Tax rate is 25%.

questions.prompt: Under AS 3, interest paid by a manufacturing company is classified as a cash flow from:
options: Either operating or investing, at the company's choice
questions.explanation: For a non-financial enterprise, interest paid is a cost of obtaining finance, so it is a financing cash flow. For a financial enterprise it is operating.

questions.prompt: Under AS 17, a segment is reportable if its revenue (external and internal) is at least what percentage of the total revenue of all segments?
questions.explanation: Each of the three tests (revenue, result, assets) uses a 10% threshold. The 75% figure is the coverage test for reportable segments' external revenue.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a related party of Alpha Ltd under AS 18?
options: A customer that buys 40% of Alpha Ltd's output, with no ownership or management link
The managing director of Alpha Ltd
questions.explanation: A single customer with whom an enterprise does a large volume of business is not a related party merely because of economic dependence. Holding companies, KMP and associates are related parties.

questions.prompt: Under AS 19, at the inception of a finance lease the lessee recognises the asset and liability at:
options: The lower of the fair value of the leased asset and the present value of minimum lease payments
The total of undiscounted minimum lease payments
Fair value of the leased asset in all cases
questions.explanation: The lessee records the lower of fair value and PV of minimum lease payments. Expensing rentals applies to operating leases.

questions.prompt: Under AS 25, income tax expense for an interim period is recognised using the estimated weighted average annual effective income tax rate expected for the full year.
questions.explanation: Income tax is assessed on annual income, so AS 25 applies the expected annual effective rate to interim pre-tax income.

questions.prompt: For a trading company, which of these are cash flows from operating activities under AS 3? Select all that apply.
options: Income tax paid, not specifically linked to investing or financing
questions.explanation: Customer receipts, supplier payments and general income tax are operating. Machinery and dividends received are investing; share issue is financing.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under AS 20, the rights issue adjustment factor = fair value per share immediately before the exercise of rights / theoretical ___ fair value per share.
questions.explanation: The theoretical ex-rights fair value (TERP) combines the market value of existing shares and the rights proceeds over the total shares after exercise.

questions.prompt: Compute the weighted average number of equity shares for basic EPS for 2026-27.
questions.explanation:
Bonus 1:4 on 24,00,000 shares = 6,00,000 shares, treated as outstanding from the start (factor 1.25 on all shares outstanding before the bonus).

| Shares | Working | Weighted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original | 20,00,000 x 1.25 x 12/12 | 25,00,000 |
| Fresh issue | 4,00,000 x 1.25 x 6/12 | 2,50,000 |
| **Total** | | **27,50,000** |

questions.prompt: Compute basic EPS for 2026-27. Answer in rupees to 2 decimals.
Compute diluted EPS for 2026-27. Answer in rupees to 2 decimals.
How does the 1 January 2027 bonus issue affect the EPS reported for 2025-26 in the 2026-27 financial statements?
options: 2025-26 EPS is restated as if the bonus shares had been outstanding throughout 2025-26
2025-26 EPS is not changed because the bonus was issued in 2026-27
2025-26 EPS is restated only for 3 months
The bonus is ignored for both years because no cash was received
questions.explanation: A bonus issue changes shares without changing resources, so AS 20 adjusts all periods presented as if it had occurred at the start of the earliest period.

questions.prompt: Identify the reportable segments under AS 17. All revenue is from external customers.
questions.answer:
**Thresholds**

- Revenue: 10% of 1,000 = 100.
- Result: total profits = 80 + 12 + 40 + 18 = 150; total losses = 30. Greater = 150; 10% = 15.
- Assets: 10% of 1,000 = 100.

| Segment | Revenue test | Result test | Assets test | Reportable? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Yes (400) | Yes (80) | Yes (500) | Yes |
| B | No (60) | No (12) | No (40) | No |
| C | No (50) | Yes (30) | No (60) | Yes |
| D | Yes (290) | Yes (40) | Yes (300) | Yes |
| E | Yes (200) | Yes (18) | Yes (100) | Yes |

**75% test**: external revenue of A, C, D, E = 400 + 50 + 290 + 200 = 940, which is 94% of 1,000, above 75%. No further segment needs to be added.

Reportable segments: **A, C, D and E**. B is reported within the reconciling 'others' item.

questions.prompt: What are the major considerations in selecting and applying accounting policies under AS 1, and what must be disclosed?
questions.answer:
- Accounting policies are the specific principles and methods adopted in preparing and presenting financial statements; the choice should give a true and fair view.
- Major considerations: **prudence** (no anticipation of profits, provision for known losses on best estimates), **substance over form** (account for the economic reality, not just the legal form) and **materiality** (disclose items whose knowledge might influence users' decisions).
- All significant accounting policies should be disclosed in one place as part of the financial statements.
- A change in policy with a material effect is disclosed with its amount (or the fact that it cannot be ascertained).
- If going concern, consistency or accrual is not followed, the fact is disclosed; if followed, no disclosure is needed.
- Disclosure of a wrong or inappropriate treatment does not rectify it.

chapters.title: Financial Statements of Companies (Schedule III)
chapters.summary: Prepare a company's Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss in the Division I format of Schedule III, with correct current and non-current classification.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act, 2013 (sections 129 and 133) and Schedule III Division I as amended by MCA, including the 2021 amendments

lesson.heading: Legal framework and Division I
lesson.body:
Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires financial statements to give a **true and fair view**, comply with the notified Accounting Standards, and follow the form in **Schedule III**.

| Division | Applies to |
| --- | --- |
| Division I | Companies following Accounting Standards (Companies (AS) Rules, 2021) |
| Division II | Ind AS companies other than NBFCs |
| Division III | NBFCs following Ind AS |

This paper uses **Division I**. Notes to accounts give the detail behind each line. Accounting Standards override Schedule III where they require a different treatment or disclosure.

**Rounding off** (Division I): companies with turnover below ₹100 crore round to the nearest hundreds, thousands, lakhs or millions (or decimals); turnover of ₹100 crore or more, to lakhs, millions or crores (or decimals). The same unit is used throughout.

lesson.heading: Balance Sheet format and classification
lesson.body:
| Heading | Main line items |
| --- | --- |
| Shareholders' funds | Share capital; Reserves and surplus; Money received against share warrants |
| Share application money pending allotment | Shown separately |
| Non-current liabilities | Long-term borrowings; Deferred tax liabilities (net); Other long-term liabilities; Long-term provisions |
| Current liabilities | Short-term borrowings; Trade payables (MSE and others); Other current liabilities; Short-term provisions |
| Non-current assets | PPE and intangible assets (including CWIP and intangibles under development); Non-current investments; DTA (net); Long-term loans and advances; Other non-current assets |
| Current assets | Current investments; Inventories; Trade receivables; Cash and cash equivalents; Short-term loans and advances; Other current assets |

An asset is **current** if it is expected to be realised in, or held for sale or consumption in, the normal operating cycle; is held mainly for trading; is expected to be realised within 12 months after the reporting date; or is cash or cash equivalent not restricted. A liability is **current** if it is expected to be settled in the operating cycle, held for trading, due within 12 months, or the company has no unconditional right to defer settlement for at least 12 months. If the operating cycle cannot be identified, it is assumed to be **12 months**.

After the 2021 amendments, **current maturities of long-term borrowings** are shown under **short-term borrowings**. Notes also include ageing of trade receivables and trade payables and shareholding of promoters.

lesson.heading: Statement of Profit and Loss
lesson.body:
| Line | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue from operations | Sale of products, services, other operating revenue |
| Other income | Interest, dividend, profit on sale of investments |
| **Total income** | |
| Cost of materials consumed | Opening RM + purchases (with direct costs) - closing RM |
| Purchases of stock-in-trade | Goods bought for resale |
| Changes in inventories of FG, WIP and stock-in-trade | Opening - closing |
| Employee benefits expense | Salaries, contribution to funds, staff welfare |
| Finance costs | Interest, other borrowing costs |
| Depreciation and amortisation expense | |
| Other expenses | |
| **Profit before exceptional and extraordinary items and tax** | |
| Exceptional items, extraordinary items, tax expense (current and deferred) | |
| **Profit for the period**, then EPS (basic and diluted) | |

**Dividends**: a final dividend proposed after the balance sheet date is not a liability (AS 4); it is disclosed in the notes. Interim dividend paid during the year is an appropriation from surplus.

lesson.heading: Worked example: classification
lesson.body:
| Item at 31 March 2027 | Classification |
| --- | --- |
| 10% term loan ₹30,00,000, ₹6,00,000 repayable in 2027-28 | Long-term borrowings ₹24,00,000; short-term borrowings (current maturities) ₹6,00,000 |
| Interest accrued but not due on the loan | Other current liabilities |
| Unpaid dividend | Other current liabilities |
| Capital advance for machinery | Long-term loans and advances |
| Provision for tax (net of advance tax) | Short-term provisions |

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Leaving the current portion of a term loan inside long-term borrowings.
- Showing a proposed final dividend as a short-term provision.
- Netting off items that Schedule III shows separately, such as trade receivables and trade payables.
- Putting capital advances in short-term loans and advances.
- Showing share application money pending allotment under share capital or current liabilities. It has its own line (amounts due for refund go to other current liabilities).
- Mixing rounding units across statements.

keyPoints: Section 129: true and fair view, comply with AS, form in Schedule III; Division I for AS companies.
Operating cycle not identifiable: assume 12 months.
Current maturities of long-term borrowings go under short-term borrowings.
Interest accrued, unpaid dividends: other current liabilities.
Capital advances: long-term loans and advances.
Proposed dividend after the reporting date: disclosed in notes, not a liability.
Rounding: turnover below ₹100 crore to hundreds/thousands/lakhs/millions; ₹100 crore or more to lakhs/millions/crores.

options: Companies whose financial statements follow the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021

options: The period of the longest contract

options: Nearest hundreds, thousands, lakhs or millions, or decimals thereof
No rounding is allowed below ₹100 crore turnover

chapters.title: Buyback of Securities
chapters.summary: Apply the buyback limits of sections 68 to 70 of the Companies Act, 2013, compute the maximum shares a company can buy back, and pass the journal entries including the Capital Redemption Reserve.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act, 2013 sections 68, 69 and 70 as in force in 2026

lesson.heading: Sources and conditions (section 68)
Capital Redemption Reserve and prohibitions (sections 69, 70)
lesson.body:
**Section 69**: where shares are bought back out of **free reserves or securities premium**, a sum equal to the **nominal value** of the shares bought back is transferred to the **Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR)**. If part of the buyback is financed by a fresh issue, the CRR = nominal value bought back - proceeds of the fresh issue used. CRR can be used only to issue fully paid bonus shares.

**Section 70**: no buyback through a subsidiary or an investment company, and none while the company is in default in repaying deposits, interest, redeeming debentures or preference shares, or repaying term loans (default must be remedied and 3 years must pass), or has failed to file the annual return, pay declared dividend or file financial statements.

**The three ICAI tests** for the maximum buyback:

| Test | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Shares outstanding test | 25% of equity shares outstanding |
| Resources test | 25% of (paid-up capital + free reserves, including securities premium) / buyback price |
| Debt-equity test | Post-buyback debt not more than 2 x (paid-up capital + free reserves) |

The **lowest** of the three is the maximum number of shares.

lesson.heading: Journal entries
lesson.body:
Example: 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 bought back at ₹30. Securities premium ₹4,00,000; general reserve ₹20,00,000.

| Entry | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equity shares buy-back A/c Dr | 15,00,000 | |
| To Bank A/c | | 15,00,000 |
| Equity share capital A/c Dr | 5,00,000 | |
| Securities premium A/c Dr | 4,00,000 | |
| General reserve A/c Dr | 6,00,000 | |
| To Equity shares buy-back A/c | | 15,00,000 |
| General reserve A/c Dr | 5,00,000 | |
| To Capital redemption reserve A/c | | 5,00,000 |

The premium of ₹10,00,000 (₹20 x 50,000) is set off first against securities premium and then free reserves. The CRR equals the nominal value of ₹5,00,000 because the buyback is out of reserves.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Excluding securities premium from the resources test. ICAI includes it with free reserves.
- Including revaluation reserve or capital reserve in free reserves. They are not free.
- Forgetting the CRR transfer, or transferring the full buyback price instead of the nominal value.
- Using pre-buyback equity in the debt-equity test. The test is on post-buyback figures.
- Allowing a buyback out of proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares.

keyPoints: Sources: free reserves, securities premium, proceeds of a different kind of security.
Board resolution up to 10%; special resolution up to 25% of paid-up capital + free reserves.
Equity buyback in a year: up to 25% of paid-up equity capital.
Post-buyback debt-equity not above 2:1.
Section 69: transfer nominal value of shares bought out of free reserves or securities premium to CRR.
Complete within 1 year; destroy within 7 days; no same-kind fresh issue for 6 months.
Maximum buyback = lowest of shares outstanding, resources and debt-equity tests.

25% of total paid-up equity capital and free reserves
No buyback can be approved by the board alone
questions.explanation: Section 68 lets the board authorise a buyback up to 10% of paid-up equity capital and free reserves. Above that, up to 25%, a special resolution is needed.

questions.prompt: When shares are bought back out of free reserves, section 69 requires a transfer to the Capital Redemption Reserve equal to:
options: The nominal value of the shares bought back
questions.explanation: The CRR replaces the capital cancelled, so it equals the nominal (face) value of shares bought back out of free reserves or securities premium.

options: Proceeds of an earlier issue of equity shares
Proceeds of a fresh issue of preference shares

questions.prompt: List the conditions in section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 that a company must satisfy for a buyback of its shares.
questions.answer:
- Buyback must be authorised by the articles of association.
- A special resolution in general meeting is needed; up to 10% of paid-up equity capital and free reserves can be approved by a board resolution.
- Buyback must not exceed 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves; for equity shares, not more than 25% of paid-up equity capital in a financial year.
- Post-buyback debt (secured and unsecured) must not exceed twice paid-up capital and free reserves, unless a higher ratio is notified.
- All shares or specified securities bought back must be fully paid.
- Listed securities: buyback in line with SEBI regulations; others: as per prescribed rules.
- Funded from free reserves, securities premium or proceeds of a different kind of security; never proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind.
- Completed within one year of the resolution; no new buyback offer within one year of closure of the previous one.
- Securities bought back are extinguished and physically destroyed within 7 days; no further issue of the same kind for 6 months except bonus and existing conversion obligations.

chapters.title: Internal Reconstruction
chapters.summary: Account for alteration and reduction of share capital, sacrifices by shareholders and creditors, and the Capital Reduction Account used to write off losses.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act, 2013 sections 48, 61, 66 and 230 as in force in 2026

lesson.heading: What internal reconstruction is
lesson.body:
**Internal reconstruction** reorganises the capital of a company that has accumulated losses, without liquidating it or forming a new company. The same company continues; shareholders (and sometimes creditors and debenture holders) accept a sacrifice so that losses and overvalued assets can be written off and the balance sheet shows a realistic position.

**External reconstruction** is different: the company is wound up and a new company takes over its business. That is accounted for as an amalgamation in the nature of purchase under AS 14.

Modes of internal reconstruction:

- **Alteration of share capital (section 61)**: consolidation, sub-division, conversion into stock, increase or cancellation of unissued shares. Needs authority in the articles and an ordinary resolution; Tribunal approval only if consolidation or division changes the voting percentage of shareholders.
- **Reduction of share capital (section 66)**: needs a **special resolution** and **confirmation by the Tribunal (NCLT)**. Capital can be reduced by extinguishing or reducing liability on uncalled capital, cancelling paid-up capital that is lost or unrepresented by available assets, or paying off capital in excess of needs.
- **Variation of shareholders' rights (section 48)** and **compromise or arrangement with creditors (section 230)**.

lesson.heading: The Capital Reduction Account
lesson.body:
All sacrifices are credited to **Capital Reduction Account** (also called Reconstruction Account). Losses and write-offs are debited to it. Any balance left is transferred to **Capital Reserve**.

| Credit side (sacrifices) | Debit side (write-offs) |
| --- | --- |
| Reduction in face value or paid-up value of shares | Debit balance of Statement of Profit and Loss |
| Creditors or debenture holders giving up part of their claim | Goodwill, patents and other intangibles without value |
| Increase in value of assets (appreciation) | Writing down overvalued PPE, inventories, receivables |
| | Reconstruction expenses |
| | Balance (if credit) to Capital Reserve |

Key entries:

| Event | Entry |
| --- | --- |
| Reduce ₹10 share to ₹4 | Equity share capital (₹10) A/c Dr; To Equity share capital (₹4) A/c; To Capital reduction A/c |
| Creditor sacrifice | Trade payables A/c Dr; To Capital reduction A/c |
| Write off losses | Capital reduction A/c Dr; To Profit and loss A/c; To Goodwill A/c; To PPE A/c |
| Surplus | Capital reduction A/c Dr; To Capital reserve A/c |

Arrears of cumulative preference dividend are not a liability, so no entry is passed when they are waived; the waiver is disclosed. If preference holders get new shares in lieu of arrears, the issue is recorded by debiting Capital Reduction Account.

lesson.heading: Worked example
lesson.body:
2,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 fully paid are reduced to ₹7 each. Trade creditors forgo ₹1,00,000. Debit balance of P&L ₹5,50,000 and plant overvaluation ₹1,50,000 are written off.

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equity share capital (₹10) A/c Dr | 20,00,000 | |
| To Equity share capital (₹7) A/c | | 14,00,000 |
| To Capital reduction A/c | | 6,00,000 |
| Trade creditors A/c Dr | 1,00,000 | |
| To Capital reduction A/c | | 1,00,000 |
| Capital reduction A/c Dr | 7,00,000 | |
| To Profit and loss A/c | | 5,50,000 |
| To Plant A/c | | 1,50,000 |

Credits ₹7,00,000 exactly match write-offs, so no capital reserve arises.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Crediting the sacrifice to the Statement of Profit and Loss or general reserve instead of Capital Reduction Account.
- Passing an entry for waived arrears of preference dividend.
- Confusing consolidation or sub-division (section 61, no change in total capital) with reduction (section 66, capital falls).
- Leaving a credit balance in Capital Reduction Account. Transfer it to Capital Reserve.
- Forgetting that NCLT confirmation is needed for a section 66 reduction.

keyPoints: Internal reconstruction: same company continues; external reconstruction: new company takes over (AS 14).
Section 61 alteration (consolidation, sub-division): ordinary resolution if articles allow.
Section 66 reduction: special resolution + NCLT confirmation.
Sacrifices credited to Capital Reduction Account; losses and overvalued assets debited.
Credit balance left in Capital Reduction Account goes to Capital Reserve.
Waiver of arrears of preference dividend: no entry, disclose.

questions.prompt: A reduction of share capital under section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires:
options: A special resolution and confirmation by the National Company Law Tribunal
A board resolution and intimation to the Registrar
Approval of SEBI for all companies
questions.explanation: Section 66 needs a special resolution and the Tribunal's confirmation, because creditors' interests are affected.

questions.prompt: Sub-division of shares of ₹10 each into shares of ₹1 each under section 61 requires:
options: Authority in the articles and an ordinary resolution in general meeting
A special resolution and NCLT confirmation
questions.explanation: Alteration under section 61 is done in general meeting if the articles authorise it; an ordinary resolution is enough. Tribunal approval is needed only if consolidation or division changes the voting percentage.

questions.prompt: After writing off losses and overvalued assets, Capital Reduction Account still has a credit balance. It is transferred to:
questions.explanation: The surplus arises from a capital sacrifice, not trading, so it is a capital profit credited to capital reserve.

questions.prompt: In internal reconstruction the existing company is liquidated and a new company is formed to take over its business.
questions.explanation: That describes external reconstruction. In internal reconstruction the same company continues, and its capital and liabilities are reorganised.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are normally debited to Capital Reduction Account? Select all that apply.
options: Debit balance of the Statement of Profit and Loss
Goodwill that has no real value
Amount by which machinery is overvalued
Reduction in the face value of equity shares
questions.explanation: Losses and the writing down of fictitious or overvalued assets are debits. Reductions in share capital and creditors' sacrifices are the credits that fund them.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the amount sacrificed by shareholders on reduction of capital is credited to ___ Account.
questions.explanation: Capital Reduction Account (also called Reconstruction Account) collects all sacrifices and is used to write off losses.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between internal reconstruction and external reconstruction.
questions.answer:
- **Entity**: in internal reconstruction the same company continues; in external reconstruction the existing company is liquidated and a new company takes over its business.
- **Law**: internal reconstruction uses sections 61 (alteration), 66 (reduction with special resolution and NCLT confirmation), 48 and 230; external reconstruction is a transfer of undertaking to a new company.
- **Accounting**: internal reconstruction uses Capital Reduction Account to write off losses and overvalued assets; external reconstruction is accounted for under AS 14 as an amalgamation in the nature of purchase, with Realisation Account in the old company's books.
- **Shareholders**: in internal reconstruction they keep shares in the same company at a reduced value; in external reconstruction they receive shares in the new company.
- **Purpose**: both give a fresh start to a loss-making business, but internal reconstruction avoids the cost of forming a new company.

chapters.title: Amalgamation of Companies (AS 14)
chapters.summary: Classify an amalgamation as merger or purchase, compute purchase consideration, and account for it in the books of the transferor and transferee companies under AS 14.
chapters.lawAsOf: AS 14 Accounting for Amalgamations as notified in the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021

lesson.heading: Merger or purchase
lesson.body:
AS 14 recognises two types of amalgamation.

**Amalgamation in the nature of merger**: all five conditions are met.

- All assets and liabilities of the transferor become those of the transferee.
- Shareholders holding at least **90% of the face value of equity shares** of the transferor (other than those already held by the transferee or its subsidiaries) become equity shareholders of the transferee.
- Consideration to those equity shareholders is discharged **wholly by issue of equity shares** of the transferee, except cash for fractional shares.
- The business of the transferor is intended to be carried on by the transferee.
- No adjustment is intended to book values, except to ensure uniform accounting policies.

**Amalgamation in the nature of purchase**: any one condition fails.

| Point | Pooling of interests (merger) | Purchase method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assets and liabilities | At existing carrying amounts (after uniform policies) | At carrying amounts or fair values |
| Reserves of transferor | Preserved in same form | Not carried, except statutory reserves |
| Difference | Adjusted in reserves | Goodwill or capital reserve |
| Goodwill | None | Amortised over not more than 5 years unless a longer period is justified |

Under purchase, **statutory reserves** of the transferor are kept by crediting the reserve and debiting **Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve**, reversed when the statutory reserve is no longer needed.

lesson.heading: Purchase consideration
lesson.body:
AS 14 defines consideration as the aggregate of shares and other securities issued and payments in cash or other assets by the transferee **to the shareholders** of the transferor. Payments to debenture holders or creditors are not part of it, and neither are the transferor's liquidation expenses borne by the transferee.

| Method | How |
| --- | --- |
| Lump sum | Given figure |
| Net payment | Shares at agreed value + cash + other securities paid to shareholders |
| Net assets | Agreed value of assets taken over - liabilities taken over |
| Share exchange / intrinsic value | Shares issued = transferor shares x (transferor value per share / transferee value per share) |

Securities issued are valued at **fair value** at the date of amalgamation.

lesson.heading: Entries in both books
lesson.body:
**Transferor (closing books)**

| Entry | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Realisation A/c Dr; To individual assets | Transfer assets at book value |
| Liabilities A/c Dr; To Realisation A/c | Transfer liabilities taken over |
| Transferee company A/c Dr; To Realisation A/c | Purchase consideration due |
| Shares in transferee, Bank Dr; To Transferee company A/c | Consideration received |
| Equity share capital, reserves Dr; To Equity shareholders A/c | Close equity |
| Realisation A/c (profit) to Equity shareholders A/c | Profit or loss on realisation |
| Equity shareholders A/c Dr; To Shares in transferee, Bank | Distribution |

**Transferee (purchase method)**

| Entry | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Business purchase A/c Dr; To Liquidator of transferor | Consideration payable |
| Assets A/c Dr (fair value); To Liabilities; To Business purchase; To Capital reserve (or Dr Goodwill) | Take over |
| Liquidator Dr; To Equity share capital; To Securities premium; To Bank | Discharge |
| Transferor's debentures Dr; To Own new debentures | Settle debenture holders |

lesson.heading: Worked example: net assets and exchange
lesson.body:
Transferor net assets at agreed values ₹60,00,000, with 4,00,000 shares; value per share ₹15. Transferee's intrinsic value per share ₹25.

Shares to be issued = 4,00,000 x 15 / 25 = **2,40,000** shares, i.e. 3 transferee shares for every 5 transferor shares. If the transferee's shares have face value ₹10 and are issued at ₹25, share capital ₹24,00,000 and securities premium ₹36,00,000 are credited, and purchase consideration is ₹60,00,000.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Including payment to debenture holders in purchase consideration.
- Treating an amalgamation as a merger when cash (beyond fractional amounts) is paid to equity shareholders.
- Carrying the transferor's general reserve into the transferee's books under the purchase method.
- Valuing shares issued at face value when the fair value (issue price) is higher; the excess is securities premium.
- Forgetting the Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve for statutory reserves under purchase.

keyPoints: Merger needs all 5 conditions: all assets/liabilities, 90% equity holders, only equity shares (cash for fractions), business continued, no book value changes.
Pooling: carrying amounts and reserves preserved; difference to reserves.
Purchase: fair or book values; excess of net assets over consideration = capital reserve; shortfall = goodwill.
Goodwill on amalgamation amortised over not more than 5 years unless longer is justified.
Purchase consideration = payments to shareholders only.
Statutory reserves under purchase: credit reserve, debit Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve.

questions.prompt: For an amalgamation in the nature of merger, shareholders holding at least what proportion of the face value of the transferor's equity shares must become equity shareholders of the transferee?
questions.explanation: AS 14 requires holders of not less than 90% of the face value of equity shares (excluding those already held by the transferee or its subsidiaries) to become equity shareholders of the transferee.

questions.prompt: Under AS 14, goodwill arising on an amalgamation in the nature of purchase should be:
options: Amortised systematically over its useful life, normally not exceeding five years unless a longer period is justified
Written off immediately against general reserve
Never amortised but tested for impairment only
Amortised over 10 years in all cases
questions.explanation: AS 14 requires amortisation over useful life, with a five-year norm unless a somewhat longer period can be justified.

questions.prompt: The transferee issues its own debentures to the transferor's debenture holders. Under AS 14 this amount is:
options: Not part of purchase consideration; it is the settlement of a liability taken over

questions.prompt: Under the pooling of interests method, the reserves of the transferor company are recorded by the transferee in the same form and at the same amounts as in the transferor's books.
questions.explanation: Pooling preserves the identity of reserves; only the difference between consideration and the transferor's share capital is adjusted in reserves.

questions.prompt: Which are recognised methods of computing purchase consideration? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Lump sum, net payment, net assets and share exchange are the four methods. Weighted average cost is an inventory formula and straight line a depreciation method.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under the purchase method, to preserve a statutory reserve of the transferor, the transferee credits that reserve and debits ___ Reserve.
questions.explanation: The Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve offsets the statutory reserve and is reversed once the statutory requirement ends.
