questions.prompt: Distinguish between the pooling of interests method and the purchase method under AS 14.
questions.answer:
- **Applicability**: pooling applies to an amalgamation in the nature of merger (all five conditions met); purchase applies when any condition fails.
- **Assets and liabilities**: pooling records them at existing carrying amounts (adjusted only for uniform policies); purchase records them at existing carrying amounts or allocates consideration on fair values.
- **Reserves**: pooling keeps the transferor's reserves in the same form; purchase does not carry them, except statutory reserves kept through the Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve.
- **Difference**: under pooling, the difference between consideration and transferor share capital goes to reserves; under purchase, the excess of consideration over net assets is goodwill (amortised, normally within five years) and a shortfall is capital reserve.
- **Consideration**: merger needs equity shares only (cash for fractions); purchase may include cash and other securities.
- **Nature**: pooling treats the combination as a union of shareholders' interests; purchase treats it as one company acquiring another.

chapters.title: Branch Accounting including Foreign Branches (AS 11)
chapters.summary: Account for dependent branches with goods at cost or invoice price, reconcile independent branches, and translate foreign branch trial balances under AS 11.
chapters.lawAsOf: AS 11 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates as notified in the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021

lesson.heading: Dependent branches and invoice price
lesson.body:
A **dependent branch** does not keep a full set of books; the head office (HO) records its results. Methods:

- **Debtors method**: a Branch Account in HO books (nominal in nature) collects opening balances, goods sent, expenses and closing balances; the balance is branch profit.
- **Stock and debtors method**: separate Branch Stock, Branch Debtors, Branch Expenses, Branch Adjustment (gross profit) and Branch P&L accounts. Useful for finding shortages.
- **Final accounts method**: a branch trading and P&L account.

Goods are often sent at **invoice price** (cost plus a mark-up) to control stock. The mark-up (**loading**) is removed through a **stock reserve** so that profit is not overstated.

| Mark-up on cost | Loading as % of invoice price |
| --- | --- |
| 25% | 25/125 = 20% |
| 33.33% | 33.33/133.33 = 25% |
| 50% | 50/150 = 33.33% |

**Shortage** = Opening stock + goods received - returns - sales - closing stock (all at invoice price). Normal loss is part of cost; abnormal shortage at cost is charged to Branch P&L.

lesson.heading: Independent branches
lesson.body:
An **independent branch** keeps its own books. HO keeps a Branch Account; the branch keeps a Head Office Account. They should mirror each other.

Before incorporation the two are **reconciled** for items recorded by one side only:

- **Goods in transit** from HO to branch: entry in branch books, debiting Goods-in-transit and crediting HO account.
- **Cash in transit**: same, in the receiving office's books.
- **HO expenses charged to branch** (depreciation of branch assets kept in HO books, share of HO overheads): branch debits the expense and credits HO account.

The branch trial balance is then **incorporated** into HO books: branch revenue and expense items through Branch Trading and P&L, assets and liabilities brought in, and the branch account closed.

lesson.heading: Foreign branches under AS 11
lesson.body:
AS 11 classifies a foreign branch as an **integral foreign operation** (its activities are an extension of the reporting enterprise, so exchange changes affect HO cash flows directly) or a **non-integral foreign operation** (largely independent, financed mainly by its own operations or local borrowings, with its own sales and costs in local currency).

| Item | Integral | Non-integral |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monetary items (cash, receivables, payables, loans) | Closing rate | Closing rate |
| Non-monetary items at historical cost (PPE, inventory at cost) | Rate on date of transaction (historical) | Closing rate |
| Depreciation | Rate used for the related asset | Rate on transaction date or average |
| Income and expenses | Rate on transaction date (average as approximation) | Rate on transaction date (average as approximation) |
| Goods from HO / HO account | Actual rupee figures in HO books | Rupee figures as in HO books |
| Exchange difference | Profit or loss | Foreign currency translation reserve until disposal |

Opening and closing stock in an integral branch are at the rates when the stock was acquired (often the opening and closing rate respectively, if so stated).

lesson.heading: Worked example: stock reserve
lesson.body:
Goods are sent to a branch at cost + 25%. Closing branch stock at invoice price is ₹1,25,000.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Closing stock at invoice price | 1,25,000 |
| Loading = 1,25,000 x 25/125 | 25,000 |
| Closing stock at cost | 1,00,000 |

Entry at year end: Branch Stock Reserve is credited with ₹25,000 (debit Branch Adjustment A/c or Branch A/c), so the stock is effectively at cost in the HO balance sheet.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Taking loading as 25% of invoice price when the mark-up is 25% on cost. It is 20%.
- Translating fixed assets of an integral branch at the closing rate.
- Recording goods in transit in HO books instead of the branch books.
- Taking exchange differences of a non-integral branch to profit or loss. They go to the foreign currency translation reserve.
- Translating HO account and goods from HO at an exchange rate instead of using the HO book figures.

keyPoints: Loading on invoice price = mark-up / (100 + mark-up).
Stock reserve removes unrealised loading on branch stock.
Goods or cash in transit: adjust in the receiving office's books (usually the branch).
AS 11 integral: monetary at closing rate, non-monetary at historical rate, revenue at average; difference to P&L.
AS 11 non-integral: assets and liabilities at closing rate, revenue at average; difference to FCTR.
HO account and goods from HO use the rupee figures in HO books.

Rewa Textiles sends goods to its Navsari branch at cost plus 25%. All branch expenses are paid by HO. Data for 2026-27 (stock figures at invoice price):

options: The exchange rate on the date the machinery was acquired
The average rate for the year
The opening rate for the year
questions.explanation: Machinery is a non-monetary item carried at historical cost, so for an integral operation it uses the rate on the transaction date.

options: Accumulated in a foreign currency translation reserve until disposal of the net investment
Recognised in profit or loss immediately
Adjusted in the cost of fixed assets
questions.explanation: For a non-integral operation, translation differences do not affect HO cash flows directly, so they go to a reserve and are recognised in profit or loss on disposal.

options: The branch books, debiting Goods-in-transit A/c and crediting Head Office A/c
The HO books, by reversing the goods sent
Both books, by cancelling the dispatch
questions.explanation: HO has already recorded the dispatch. The branch, which has not recorded it, passes the entry so the HO and branch accounts agree.

questions.prompt: Which feature indicates that a foreign branch is a non-integral foreign operation?
options: It generates its own sales and costs in local currency and is financed mainly by its own operations or local borrowings
It only sells goods imported from HO and remits the proceeds to HO

It acts as an extension of HO's operations
questions.explanation: A high degree of autonomy, local financing and local transactions point to a non-integral operation. The others describe an integral operation.

questions.explanation: The rate on the transaction date is required, but an average rate is allowed as a practical approximation.

questions.prompt: Compute the net profit of the Navsari branch for 2026-27. Answer in rupees.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between integral and non-integral foreign operations under AS 11 and how each is translated.
questions.answer:
- An **integral foreign operation** carries on business as if it were an extension of the reporting enterprise; a change in exchange rate affects the reporting enterprise's cash flows almost immediately. Example: a branch that sells goods imported from HO and remits proceeds.
- A **non-integral foreign operation** accumulates cash and other monetary items, incurs expenses, generates income and arranges borrowings mainly in its local currency, with a high degree of autonomy.
- **Integral translation**: as if the transactions were HO's own; monetary items at closing rate, non-monetary items at historical cost at transaction-date rates, income and expenses at transaction-date (or average) rates; exchange differences to profit or loss.
- **Non-integral translation**: all assets and liabilities at closing rate; income and expenses at transaction-date (or average) rates; exchange differences to foreign currency translation reserve until disposal of the net investment, when they are recycled to profit or loss.
- Indicators: control by HO, proportion of transactions with HO, financing source, and whether local or HO currency drives sales prices and costs.

chapters.title: Consolidated Financial Statements (AS 21, 23, 27)
chapters.summary: Prepare a consolidated balance sheet for a holding company with one subsidiary under AS 21: cost of control, minority interest, pre- and post-acquisition profits and intra-group eliminations, with an overview of AS 23 and AS 27.
chapters.lawAsOf: AS 21, AS 23 and AS 27 as notified in the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021; section 129(3) of the Companies Act, 2013

lesson.heading: Control and scope of AS 21
lesson.body:
Section 129(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires a company with subsidiaries to prepare consolidated financial statements (CFS) in addition to its own. Under **AS 21**, a **subsidiary** is an enterprise **controlled** by the parent. Control means:

- ownership, directly or through subsidiaries, of **more than one-half of the voting power**; or
- control of the **composition of the board of directors** (or governing body) so as to obtain economic benefits from its activities.

A subsidiary is **excluded** from consolidation only when control is intended to be **temporary** (acquired and held exclusively with a view to subsequent disposal in the near future) or when it operates under **severe long-term restrictions** that significantly impair its ability to transfer funds to the parent. Such an investment is accounted for under AS 13, with reasons disclosed.

The parent and subsidiary use **uniform accounting policies**. If reporting dates differ, adjustments are made for significant transactions, and the difference cannot exceed **six months**.

lesson.heading: Consolidation procedure
lesson.body:
Line-by-line addition of assets, liabilities, income and expenses, then:

| Step | Working |
| --- | --- |
| Cost of control | Cost of investment - parent's share of subsidiary's equity (capital + reserves) at the **date of acquisition**. Positive = goodwill; negative = capital reserve |
| Minority interest | Minority's share of subsidiary's equity at the **reporting date** (capital + all reserves, pre and post) |
| Group reserves | Parent's own reserves + parent's share of subsidiary's **post-acquisition** profits and reserves |
| Eliminations | Intra-group balances (receivables/payables, loans), intra-group sales and purchases, and **unrealised profits** on intra-group stock, in full |

Pre-acquisition profits are capital profits (go into cost of control). Post-acquisition profits are revenue profits, shared between group and minority. When a subsidiary is acquired during a year, profit for that year is split by time (unless otherwise stated).

**Minority interests** are presented in the consolidated balance sheet separately from liabilities and from the equity of the parent's shareholders.

Unrealised profit on stock sold by parent to subsidiary at cost plus a mark-up: closing stock x mark-up / (100 + mark-up).

lesson.heading: AS 23 and AS 27 overview
lesson.body:
**AS 23 Investments in associates in CFS**: an **associate** is an enterprise in which the investor has **significant influence** (power to participate in financial and operating policy decisions, not control). Holding **20% or more** of voting power presumes significant influence unless shown otherwise. The associate is accounted for by the **equity method**: the investment is recorded at cost (goodwill or capital reserve identified within it) and adjusted for the investor's share of post-acquisition profits or losses; dividends received reduce the carrying amount.

**AS 27 Financial reporting of interests in joint ventures**: in CFS, a venturer reports its interest in a **jointly controlled entity** using **proportionate consolidation**: its share of each asset, liability, income and expense is combined line by line. In its separate statements, the interest is an investment under AS 13.

| Investee | Relationship | Method in CFS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subsidiary | Control | Full consolidation (AS 21) |
| Associate | Significant influence | Equity method (AS 23) |
| Jointly controlled entity | Joint control | Proportionate consolidation (AS 27) |

lesson.heading: Worked example
lesson.body:
H Ltd acquired 60% of S Ltd on 1 April 2026 for ₹9,00,000. S Ltd at acquisition: share capital ₹10,00,000, reserves ₹2,00,000. At 31 March 2027: share capital ₹10,00,000, reserves ₹2,00,000, P&L (post-acquisition) ₹3,00,000. H Ltd's own P&L balance is ₹8,00,000.

| Working | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Net assets at acquisition | 12,00,000 |
| H's share 60% | 7,20,000 |
| **Goodwill** (9,00,000 - 7,20,000) | **1,80,000** |
| **Minority interest** 40% x 15,00,000 | **6,00,000** |
| Group share of post-acquisition profit 60% x 3,00,000 | 1,80,000 |
| **Consolidated P&L** (8,00,000 + 1,80,000) | **9,80,000** |

The subsidiary's share capital and reserves do not appear separately in the consolidated balance sheet; they are absorbed into cost of control, minority interest and group reserves.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Computing minority interest on equity at acquisition date. Use equity at the reporting date.
- Treating all of the subsidiary's reserves as post-acquisition.
- Eliminating only the parent's share of unrealised profit on downstream sales. AS 21 eliminates unrealised profit in full.
- Showing minority interest within liabilities or within the parent's equity.
- Excluding a subsidiary just because its business is different from the parent's. That is not a ground for exclusion.

keyPoints: Subsidiary: more than half of voting power, or control of board composition.
Exclude only for temporary control or severe long-term restrictions on fund transfer.
Goodwill/capital reserve = cost of investment - parent's share of equity at acquisition.
Minority interest = minority share of equity at the reporting date; shown separately from liabilities and parent's equity.
Unrealised profit on intra-group stock eliminated in full: stock x mark-up / (100 + mark-up).
Reporting date gap up to 6 months; uniform accounting policies.
AS 23 associate (20%+, significant influence): equity method. AS 27 JCE: proportionate consolidation.

cases.title: Case: Ganga Ltd and Yamuna Ltd
cases.body:
On 1 April 2026 Ganga Ltd acquired 80,000 of the 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each of Yamuna Ltd for ₹16,00,000.

| Yamuna Ltd | 1 April 2026 (₹) | 31 March 2027 (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Share capital | 10,00,000 | 10,00,000 |
| General reserve | 4,00,000 | 4,00,000 |
| Profit and loss (credit) | 2,00,000 | 5,00,000 |

During 2026-27 Ganga Ltd sold goods to Yamuna Ltd at cost plus 25%. Yamuna Ltd's closing stock includes ₹1,00,000 of these goods (at invoice price). Ganga Ltd's own Profit and loss balance at 31 March 2027 is ₹12,00,000. No dividends were declared.

questions.prompt: Under AS 21, an enterprise is a subsidiary of another when the other enterprise:
options: Owns more than one-half of its voting power, directly or through subsidiaries, or controls the composition of its board
Owns 20% or more of its voting power
Shares joint control with another venturer
questions.explanation: Control under AS 21 is more than half of voting power or control of board composition. 20% indicates significant influence (associate, AS 23); joint control is AS 27.

questions.prompt: Under AS 23, holding what proportion of voting power presumes significant influence over an investee?
questions.explanation: AS 23 presumes significant influence at 20% or more of voting power, unless it can be clearly shown otherwise.

questions.prompt: In consolidated financial statements, AS 27 requires a venturer's interest in a jointly controlled entity to be reported using:
options: Cost less provision for permanent decline
questions.explanation: AS 27 uses proportionate consolidation in CFS: the venturer combines its share of each item line by line.

questions.prompt: Under AS 21, the financial statements of a subsidiary may be drawn up to a different reporting date, provided the difference does not exceed six months and adjustments are made for significant transactions.
questions.explanation: AS 21 allows a different reporting date of up to six months, with adjustments for significant intervening transactions or events.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are eliminated in preparing consolidated financial statements under AS 21? Select all that apply.
options: Sales by the subsidiary to outside customers
Minority's share of the subsidiary's reserves
questions.explanation: Intra-group balances, transactions and unrealised profits are eliminated in full. Sales to outsiders stay; the minority's share of reserves goes into minority interest.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: when the parent's share of the subsidiary's equity at acquisition exceeds the cost of investment, the difference is shown in the consolidated balance sheet as ___.
questions.explanation: A negative cost of control is a capital reserve; a positive one is goodwill.

questions.prompt: Compute goodwill (cost of control) on acquisition of Yamuna Ltd. Answer in rupees.
Compute minority interest at 31 March 2027. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: Equity at 31 March 2027 = 10,00,000 + 4,00,000 + 5,00,000 = ₹19,00,000. Minority 20% = **₹3,80,000**. The unrealised profit relates to a downstream sale (Ganga to Yamuna), so it does not affect the minority.

questions.prompt: What unrealised profit must be eliminated from the consolidated closing stock?
questions.explanation: Unrealised profit = 1,00,000 x 25/125 = ₹20,000, eliminated in full from consolidated stock and group profit.

questions.prompt: Compute the consolidated Profit and loss balance at 31 March 2027. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation:
Post-acquisition profit of Yamuna = 5,00,000 - 2,00,000 = ₹3,00,000; Ganga's 80% share = ₹2,40,000.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Ganga Ltd's own P&L | 12,00,000 |
| Add: Share of Yamuna's post-acquisition profit | 2,40,000 |
| Less: Unrealised profit on stock | (20,000) |
| **Consolidated P&L** | **14,20,000** |

questions.prompt: H Ltd acquired 75% of S Ltd on 1 July 2026. S Ltd earned a profit of ₹12,00,000 evenly during 2026-27 (year ending 31 March 2027). Compute H Ltd's share of S Ltd's post-acquisition profit for the year. Answer in rupees.
questions.explanation: Pre-acquisition (April to June) = 12,00,000 x 3/12 = ₹3,00,000. Post-acquisition = ₹9,00,000. H's share = 75% x 9,00,000 = **₹6,75,000**.

questions.prompt: Under AS 21, minority interests in the consolidated balance sheet are presented:
options: Separately from liabilities and from the equity of the parent's shareholders
As part of the parent's reserves and surplus
questions.explanation: AS 21 requires minority interests to be shown separately from both liabilities and the parent shareholders' equity.

questions.prompt: Compute goodwill or capital reserve, minority interest and consolidated reserves, and show the relevant extract of the consolidated balance sheet of P Ltd at 31 March 2027.
questions.data:
P Ltd acquired 90,000 of the 1,20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each of Q Ltd on 1 April 2026 for ₹12,00,000.

| Q Ltd | 1 April 2026 (₹) | 31 March 2027 (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Share capital | 12,00,000 | 12,00,000 |
| General reserve | 3,00,000 | 3,00,000 |
| Profit and loss | 1,00,000 | 5,00,000 |

P Ltd: share capital ₹50,00,000, general reserve ₹10,00,000, P&L ₹15,00,000. No intra-group transactions.
questions.answer:
Holding = 90,000 / 1,20,000 = 75%; minority 25%.

**Analysis of Q Ltd's equity**

| Item | Total (₹) | Pre-acquisition (₹) | Post-acquisition (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Share capital | 12,00,000 | 12,00,000 | |
| General reserve | 3,00,000 | 3,00,000 | |
| Profit and loss | 5,00,000 | 1,00,000 | 4,00,000 |
| **Total** | **20,00,000** | **16,00,000** | **4,00,000** |
| P Ltd 75% | | 12,00,000 | 3,00,000 |
| Minority 25% | 5,00,000 (on total) | | |

**Cost of control**: Cost 12,00,000 - 75% of 16,00,000 (12,00,000) = **Nil** (no goodwill, no capital reserve).

**Minority interest** = 25% x 20,00,000 = **₹5,00,000**.

**Consolidated P&L** = 15,00,000 + 3,00,000 = **₹18,00,000**. Consolidated general reserve = P Ltd's ₹10,00,000 (Q's general reserve is all pre-acquisition).

**Extract: Consolidated Balance Sheet of P Ltd as at 31 March 2027**

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Share capital | 50,00,000 |
| Reserves and surplus: General reserve 10,00,000; P&L 18,00,000 | 28,00,000 |
| Minority interest | 5,00,000 |

questions.prompt: When can a subsidiary be excluded from consolidation under AS 21, and how is it then accounted for?
questions.answer:
- AS 21 allows exclusion only in two cases: (a) control is intended to be temporary because the subsidiary was acquired and is held exclusively with a view to its subsequent disposal in the near future; (b) the subsidiary operates under severe long-term restrictions that significantly impair its ability to transfer funds to the parent.
- An excluded subsidiary is accounted for as an investment under AS 13.
- The reasons for not consolidating are disclosed in the CFS.
- A subsidiary is not excluded merely because its business activities are dissimilar from those of other group members; relevant information is given through segment disclosures.
- Section 129(3) separately requires CFS for companies with subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures, so the exclusion is narrow.
